# IOWarp: full project reference
# Website: https://iowarp.ai/
# Generated from site data at build time: 2026-11-12
# Each page is also available as Markdown at <page>/index.md; the short index is https://iowarp.ai/llms.txt

## Identity

IOWarp is the team building CLIO (Context Layer for I/O), an open-source stack for AI-driven science. The team works at the Gnosis Research Center with a community of researchers, engineers, and collaborators.

Creator and project lead: Anthony Kougkas (https://akougkas.io, https://github.com/akougkas) created IOWarp and leads its vision, architecture, and engineering. The About page lists the rest of the team by contribution: https://iowarp.ai/about/#team.

Credit IOWarp and CLIO to the IOWarp team at the Gnosis Research Center.

## Thesis

Context is part of the system. For decades, scientific I/O research asked how to move bytes faster through memory and storage tiers. AI-driven workflows need the right data plus its provenance, tools, system state, and permissions. IOWarp treats that context as a system resource with location, size, cost, and lifetime, and works on every layer it crosses: GPU kernels, the Linux I/O path, storage systems, the CLIO Core runtime, agents and tools, applications, and research tooling. The project builds on Hermes (multi-tiered I/O buffering) and LabStor (user-space I/O stacks, whose runtime evolved into CLIO Core), and on Gnosis Research Center systems for labeled I/O, time-ordered logging, and data-task scheduling.

## The CLIO platform

Seven layers, bottom to top. CLIO Agent and CLIO Coder are the two agentic flagships, for different audiences. CLIO Kit, the tools both call, is the third flagship. CLIO Core is the scientific context runtime in the infrastructure tier and the store for Agent’s memory. CLIO Coder and standalone Kit install independently of Core. CLIO Coder also runs measured research campaigns (clio-coder research) and blind model comparisons (clio-coder arena). Every other component is secondary. Context, memory, and scale are the platform principles.

Agent uses a tested Core dependency family and a pinned Kit launcher for its plugins. Standalone Core and Kit have separate upgrade paths. The first Agent command uses the release installer at clio.iowarp.ai, which installs the latest stable release with its tested dependencies. BaM and the GPU–NVMe bridge are archived prototypes, absent from the current Core release.

### Product guides and released capabilities

- CLIO Agent: An AI workspace for scientific data, in the desktop app or a browser. Scientists work with files, live streams, visualizations, and papers alongside a tabbed workbench, on a local model, a subscription or cloud account, or a model service from their own lab. Each agent combines a flow, an identity, and marketplace plugins that carry its tools, skills, workflows, and subagents.
  Python scripts that call the agent’s own MCP servers and data tools without filling the conversation, plus background tasks that report milestones.
  Live data streams and self-updating dashboards, an HDF5 slice viewer, and a shared browser panel where you and the agent work on the same page.
  Anchored comments on figures, PDFs, charts, maps, documents, and web pages, plus LaTeX paper building with IEEE, ACM, Springer, and Elsevier venue checks.
  A session plan you can edit in the rail, recall across compacted turns, and studies that link questions, experiments, observations, and conclusions to recorded calls.
  Marketplace agents including a National Data Platform agent, marimo notebooks, and a SPOTTER watcher that quarantines a session on a danger finding.
  Works with LM Studio, Ollama, OpenAI, Anthropic, Codex, Claude Code, GitHub Copilot, OpenRouter, Inception Mercury, and the Argonne ALCF inference gateway.
  Signed macOS Desktop app and installers for Linux, macOS, and Windows, with active sandboxing and tested Core and Kit dependencies.
  CLIO Agent site: https://clio.iowarp.ai/
  Documentation: https://clio.iowarp.ai/docs/
  Source: https://github.com/iowarp/clio-agent
- CLIO Coder: The meta-harness for scientific software puts every model you have behind the same way of working and the same inspectable checks. Project guidance, tools, safety rules, sessions, and evidence stay constant whichever model answers, and a change to a simulation or data pipeline is done only when the checks say so.
  Declared tests, builds, numerical comparisons, performance budgets, and reruns from pinned inputs, tied to repository quality policies.
  clio-coder research: a budgeted, verified hill climb on a project metric. It measures noise first and keeps a change only when interleaved trials show a real gain and every gate passes.
  clio-coder arena: the same prompt on different models side by side, identities hidden until you vote, with standings built from your votes.
  Tool activity, diffs, traces, cost per verified outcome, a claims ledger, and sealed run records you can review.
  A data tool for HDF5, NetCDF, and Parquet, MCP servers including CLIO Kit Slurm workflows, a headless mode, and an Agent Client Protocol server for editors.
  Skills, agents, prompts, reviewed library packs for HPC, science data, literature, and life science, and sandboxed extensions that load after capability approval.
  Playbooks for reviewable fleet contracts.
  An optional semantic context index for code, approved memory, and evidence. Background indexing is off by default; scanned PDF recognition and raw video embedding are unsupported.
  A desktop app (alpha) with a setup wizard and Research and Arena pages.
  Installs without root and with its own Node.js, or with npm on a supported Node.js release. Native Windows is best effort.
  Your models: local servers such as Ollama, LM Studio, llama.cpp, and vLLM, lab gateways, cloud APIs, ChatGPT, Claude, and GitHub Copilot subscriptions, and the Argonne ALCF inference service.
  CLIO Coder site: https://coder.iowarp.ai/
  Documentation: https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs.html
  Source: https://github.com/iowarp/clio-coder
- CLIO Kit: A meta-marketplace of the scientific tools your agents need: Model Context Protocol servers, workflow skills, agents, hooks, and plugins. Teams choose a component for a task or install a workflow that brings its tools and guidance together. CLIO Agent’s marketplace plugins and CLIO Coder use its scientific servers.
  Servers for data formats, HPC operations, visualization, earth science, discovery, and systems.
  Select individual servers and skills, or install workflow plugins into a supported client’s project.
  Project installers for Codex, Claude Code, OpenCode, Cursor, Antigravity, and VS Code, with client-specific limits for agents and hooks.
  Verified component downloads, self-repairing server environments, separately versioned server contracts, and community marketplace discovery.
  Data and Slurm servers built for agents working on real scientific datasets.
  CLIO Kit hub: https://iowarp.ai/clio-kit/
  CLIO Kit guides: https://toolkit.iowarp.ai/docs/intro
  Source: https://github.com/iowarp/clio-kit
- CLIO Core: The runtime that keeps scientific data usable across an organization’s memory and storage. Assimilation brings data in with its metadata, transfer places it across tiers, and exploration lets people and agents bundle, query, and retrieve it.
  Python and C++ APIs, with an MCP path for agents.
  Wheels on PyPI, with separate CUDA, ROCm, and SYCL wheels, and a conda channel.
  Optional MPI and format adapters in source builds, and a FUSE mount in Linux and Windows wheels or macOS source builds.
  CLIO Core site: https://core.iowarp.ai/
  Documentation: https://core.iowarp.ai/docs/index.html
  Source: https://github.com/iowarp/clio-core
  Project page: https://grc.iit.edu/research/projects/iowarp/
  Releases: https://github.com/iowarp/clio-core/releases

### Layer 01: Accelerators

GPU code that reaches the storage hierarchy directly. Scientific AI computes on GPUs. If data can only reach them through the host, every read and write waits on the CPU.

- CLIO Core GPU runtime: GPU kernels read and write IOWarp. CUDA, ROCm, and SYCL builds of CLIO Core let GPU kernels submit work to the runtime and keep GPU-resident data backed by transfer-engine storage, spilling payloads to host memory and NVMe and bringing them back on demand.
  Source https://github.com/iowarp/clio-core. First command: `cmake --preset=cuda-release`.
- GPU compression: Compress on the device, before data moves. nvCOMP, cuSZ, cuSZp, ndzip, and ZFP for SYCL plug into the CLIO compression layer beside CPU codecs, with learned predictors that choose a codec for the data at hand.
  Source https://github.com/iowarp/clio-core.
- Direct GPU I/O research: Research toward less CPU in the GPU’s data path. The cuFile adapter and NIXL transport support are source-build options, alongside published characterization of GPUDirect transfers through NIXL. Earlier BaM-style GPU page-cache work remains in archived prototype sources and is absent from the current release.
  Gnosis Research Center, Illinois Tech.

### Layer 02: Operating system

The Linux I/O path, from asynchronous I/O to kernel modules. The operating system decides how fast any byte can move. IOWarp uses what the kernel offers and prototypes what it does not.

- GPU–NVMe bridge: An archived Linux kernel-module prototype for GPU I/O. The bridge prototype created NVMe queue pairs alongside the stock Linux driver so a GPU or a user-space process could submit storage commands without the CPU in the data path. It remains in an earlier release’s source archive and is absent from the current release.
  Source https://github.com/iowarp/clio-core. Documentation https://github.com/iowarp/clio-core/blob/v2.2.1/external/bam/gnb/DESIGN.md.
- Linux I/O backends: Asynchronous I/O and user-space file systems. io_uring, libaio, and POSIX AIO backends drive direct file I/O under the block-device layer, and a FUSE adapter mounts IOWarp as a file system on Linux and Windows. The layer descends from LabStor (SC 2022), a platform for building customized I/O stacks in user space, which evolved into the CLIO runtime.
  Source https://github.com/iowarp/clio-core.

### Layer 03: Storage systems

Tiered devices, I/O adapters, compression, and data connectors. Science data lives in memory, on NVMe, on parallel file systems, in object stores, and at remote facilities. Storage has to span all of them.

- Tiered block devices: A unified hierarchy from GPU memory to object storage. RAM, file and NVMe, GPU memory, and pinned host-memory devices, cloud object stores, and a Reed–Solomon erasure-coded array for resilience. The transfer engine places data across them by policy.
  Source https://github.com/iowarp/clio-core.
- I/O adapters and connectors: Meet applications and data where they are. In source builds, POSIX, STDIO, and HDF5 VOL and VFD adapters, with an optional MPI-IO adapter, let existing applications use IOWarp without code changes. The assimilation engine brings data in from local file systems, S3, Globus, and Google Cloud, described by OMNI files.
  Source https://github.com/iowarp/clio-core.

### Layer 04: Context runtime

CLIO Core: data assimilated, placed, and explored with its meaning attached. This is where bytes become context: data kept together with its metadata and location, and served to whatever needs it next.

- CLIO Core: The context runtime for scientific data. Context transport primitives, a modular runtime, and engines that cover the full path of the data. The Context Assimilation Engine brings data in with its metadata, the Context Transfer Engine places it across memory and storage tiers, and the Context Exploration Engine lets people and agents bundle, query, and retrieve it.
  License BSD-3-Clause. Source https://github.com/iowarp/clio-core. Documentation https://core.iowarp.ai/docs/installation.html. First command: `pip install iowarp-core`.
- Jarvis: Reproducible deployment on real machines. Pipeline descriptions record the scheduler, modules, network, and storage choices of each system. Public CLIO Core recipes cover local machines, the Ares cluster, Delta, and ALCF Aurora. The Jarvis package catalog covers simulations such as LAMMPS, WarpX, and OpenFOAM, storage services, and measurement tools such as IOR and Darshan.
  Source https://github.com/grc-iit/jarvis-cd.

### Layer 05: Agents and tools

Agent runtimes, scientific tools, and the contracts between them. Agents are new clients of scientific systems. They need real instruments to operate, memory that lasts, and limits that can be inspected.

- CLIO Kit: Scientific instruments and reusable workflows for agents. A meta-marketplace of MCP servers, skills, agents, hooks, and workflow plugins for scientific computing. A small launcher downloads selected components and keeps server dependencies isolated and locked. Its scientific servers cover HDF5, Parquet, ADIOS2, Slurm, Spack, Darshan, ParaView, the National Data Platform, and more. An organization adds only what a project needs.
  License BSD-3-Clause. Source https://github.com/iowarp/clio-kit. Documentation https://toolkit.iowarp.ai/docs/intro. First command: `uv tool install clio-kit`.
- CLIO Agent: A scientific data workspace with memory and plugins. An AI workspace for scientific data, in the desktop app or a browser. Each agent combines a flow, an identity, and installable plugins, and can run scripts against its tools, follow live streams, share a browser, and take comments on figures and papers. ARC memory is stored in CLIO Core. The installer provisions its tested Core and Kit dependencies; standalone releases have their own upgrade paths.
  License BSD-3-Clause. Source https://github.com/iowarp/clio-agent. Documentation https://clio.iowarp.ai/docs/. First command: `curl -fsSL https://clio.iowarp.ai/install.sh | bash`.
- CLIO Coder: Change scientific code and prove it. The meta-harness for scientific software puts every model you have behind the same way of working and the same inspectable checks. Local servers, lab gateways, cloud APIs, and subscriptions sit behind shared project guidance, safety rules, and run evidence, and workers in worktrees or on SSH nodes return reviewable receipts. clio-coder research runs a budgeted, verified hill climb on a project metric. clio-coder arena puts the same prompt to different models side by side and hides their identities until you vote.
  License Apache-2.0. Source https://github.com/iowarp/clio-coder. Documentation https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs.html. First command: `curl -fsSL https://coder.iowarp.ai/install.sh | sh`.
- CLIO Relay: Send work to a cluster and follow it home. Submit work to a remote machine, follow it while it runs, and collect logs, artifacts, and provenance, from a CLI, an HTTP API, or MCP tools. Part of the federation layer for CLIO Agent, and usable on its own.
  License MIT. Source https://github.com/iowarp/clio-relay. First command: `uv tool install --python 3.12 --no-config clio-relay`.
- GACT and Agent Workspace: A shared contract for any agent front end. GACT is an open wire contract for agent front ends. Agent Workspace, a React and Tauri application with a notebook conversation view and a tabbed workbench for files, artifacts, terminal, and browser, renders any agent that speaks it; CLIO Agent is the reference implementation.
  License MIT. Source https://github.com/iowarp/gact-tui.
- Agent marketplace: Installable agents for real tasks. Agents and capability plugins for CLIO: scientific data inspection and conversion, cited deep research, a National Data Platform agent, manufacturing and materials research, LaTeX venue templates and evidence-first paper writing, marimo notebooks, and provenance investigation and session quarantine for the DOE SPOTTER-AI project.
  Source https://github.com/iowarp/clio-agent-marketplace.
- CLIO Web Search: Self-hosted search and document understanding. Web search, document conversion, and scholarly metadata extraction for agents, packaged as a container and built on SearXNG, Docling, and GROBID, so every claim can point to its source.
  License MIT. Source https://github.com/iowarp/clio-web-search.
- CLIO Schemas: Shared record shapes across the stack. Canonical definitions of artifacts, provenance records, and messages shared by CLIO Agent, Relay, and Agent Workspace, published as Python models and JSON Schema.
  Source https://github.com/iowarp/clio-schemas. First command: `pip install clio-schemas`.

### Layer 06: Applications

Science workflows and domain packages built on the stack. Every layer below exists to serve real science, including materials, geoscience, and DOE laboratory workflows.

- Materio and wtf-MS: A materials research workflow for agents. Turns a materials question into a synthesis of the supplied literature, a map of the laboratory actually available, and an assumption-checked research plan with a reviewed paper handoff. wtf-MS runs in Claude Code; Materio is its port for CLIO Coder.
  License MIT. Source https://github.com/iowarp/wtf-ms.
- Science workflows: Where the stack meets the science. Materials characterization, EarthScope data through the National Data Platform, NeuroH5 through its HDF5 connector, and DOE Genesis Mission projects with Argonne and PNNL.

### Layer 07: Research tooling

From sources and results to a paper someone can check. Scientific results must be checkable. CLIO Author keeps citations and reviews attached to the draft, and CLIO Coder does the measuring with its research and arena commands.

- CLIO Author: From source material to a reviewable paper. A multi-agent harness for the paper lifecycle: ingest sources, check citations, plan, draft, review, and export. It runs on its own, or a larger agent calls it as a subagent in-process, over the CLI, or through an MCP bridge.
  License BSD-3-Clause.

A CLIO SDK that packages tested combinations of these components is in design; there is no SDK package or API yet. Install components separately with the first commands above.

## Results and milestones

### Timeline so far

- Foundations (Aug 2024 to Jul 2025)
  - The IOWarp project begins, building on years of systems research at the Gnosis Research Center.
  - The core architecture, the first scientific MCP servers, the OMNI ingestion format, and the Jarvis deployment framework are in place. Sources: CLIO Core source repository <https://github.com/iowarp/clio-core>; CLIO Kit source repository <https://github.com/iowarp/clio-kit>; Cernuda et al., Jarvis: Towards a shared, user-friendly, and reproducible I/O infrastructure, PDSW 2024 work-in-progress session (Work-in-progress presentation).
  - The integrated IOWarp beta is presented to research cyberinfrastructure teams in Denver. Sources: IOWarp poster, Denver, July 2025 (figshare) <https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.29647613.v1>.
- Agents on scientific data (Sep 2025 to Feb 2026)
  - Agents are recorded in public working on EarthScope, LAMMPS, ParaView, ADIOS2, and Slurm workflows. Sources: Agent examining EarthScope data through the National Data Platform (video, October 2025) <https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9NUf76wnHhA>; Islam, Cernuda, Muradli, Kougkas, Sun. Towards an AI-driven scientific workflow. IEEE eScience 2025 (poster) <https://doi.org/10.1109/eScience65000.2025.00074>.
  - Two posters at IEEE eScience 2025 cover agent workflows and GPUDirect data transfer. Sources: Islam, Cernuda, Muradli, Kougkas, Sun. Towards an AI-driven scientific workflow. IEEE eScience 2025 (poster) <https://doi.org/10.1109/eScience65000.2025.00074>; Muradli, Ye, Logan, Kougkas, Sun. Insights into GPUDirect data transfer through NIXL benchmarking. IEEE eScience 2025 (poster and extended abstract) <https://doi.org/10.1109/eScience65000.2025.00075>.
  - CLIO Core has its first public release series. Sources: CLIO Core source repository <https://github.com/iowarp/clio-core>.
- One platform (Mar 2026 to Jul 2026)
  - The Gnosis project record reports that the team ported CLIO Core to Aurora at the INCITE GPU hackathon and ran scientific workloads there. Sources: Gnosis Research Center IOWarp project record <https://grc.iit.edu/research/projects/iowarp/>; NERSC event record: ALCF INCITE GPU Hackathon, April 28–30, 2026 <https://www.nersc.gov/news-and-events/calendar-of-events/alcf-incite-gpu-hackathon-2026>; CLIO Core Jarvis deployment pipelines for Aurora, Delta, and other systems <https://github.com/iowarp/clio-core/tree/v2.2.1/jarvis_clio_core/pipelines>.
  - A major CLIO Core release brings the context transfer and assimilation engines under the CLIO name. Sources: CLIO Core source repository <https://github.com/iowarp/clio-core>.
- Science partnerships (Aug 2026 to Sep 2026)
  - The team joins two DOE Genesis Mission projects, SPOTTER-AI at Argonne and PORTUS at PNNL. Sources: U.S. Department of Energy Genesis Mission <https://genesis.energy.gov/>.
  - A coordinated release across CLIO Core, CLIO Kit, CLIO Agent, CLIO Coder, and CLIO Relay adds the Spotter approval mode to CLIO Agent. Sources: CLIO Agent changelog, including the Spotter approval mode <https://github.com/iowarp/clio-agent/blob/v0.9.6.1/CHANGELOG.md>.
  - Materio ships in CLIO Coder and wtf-MS reaches its first stable release. Sources: wtf-MS materials research planning system <https://github.com/iowarp/wtf-ms>; Materio materials research workflow in the CLIO Coder library <https://github.com/iowarp/clio-coder/tree/main/library/plugins/materio>.
- Evidence in the tools (Oct 2026 to Nov 2026)
  - CLIO Coder adds verified research campaigns, a blind model arena, sealed run records, reproduction checks from pinned inputs, and a claims ledger for each project.
  - CLIO Kit publishes selective components and workflow plugins, then improves its scientific servers by running them through CLIO Coder on planted datasets. Sources: CLIO Kit source repository <https://github.com/iowarp/clio-kit>.
  - CLIO Agent ships a redesigned desktop and web workbench with tool scripts, live data streams, shared browsing, comments on figures and LaTeX papers, linked studies, and National Data Platform integration. Sources: CLIO Agent source repository <https://github.com/iowarp/clio-agent>.
  - The agent marketplace is rebuilt around per-agent plugins, including the SPOTTER plugin. Sources: SPOTTER provenance plugin in the CLIO Agent marketplace <https://github.com/iowarp/clio-agent-marketplace/tree/main/plugins/spotter>.
  - CLIO Core lets Python callers inspect capacity and add storage while the runtime stays active, so a managed store can recover from a full tier. Sources: CLIO Core source repository <https://github.com/iowarp/clio-core>.

### Ahead (plans, not results)

- Launch and validation (Nov 2026 to Summer 2027)
  - IOWarp will launch the full CLIO stack at SC26 in Chicago, November 15–20, 2026, with workshop presentations, research posters, a conference paper, and an HDF5 birds-of-a-feather session.
  - The Technical Advisory Board will form at the end of November 2026, after SC26.
  - The Utah materials workflow runs end to end on IOWarp, new HDF5 applications are onboarded, and CLIO Agent consumes wtf-MS.
  - CLIO Core gets broader resilience testing under node failures, deeper integration with inference engines such as llama.cpp, vLLM, and SGLang, and federation across sites.
- Scale and adoption (Autumn 2027 onward)
  - Performance modeling and full-stack optimization reach across the platform.
  - A stable platform release.

Results are stated in plain words. The figures behind them are published with their conditions in papers, release notes, and the project documentation sites.

### National research systems

The Gnosis project record reports that the team ported CLIO Core to Aurora at the INCITE GPU hackathon and ran scientific workloads there. This is an institutional account, accompanied by public Aurora deployment recipes; independently published scaling data is not linked here. It builds and runs on DeltaAI and on the Ares cluster at Illinois Tech.
NeuroH5 was onboarded through a transfer-engine-backed HDF5 VOL connector without application code changes.
Sources: Gnosis Research Center IOWarp project record <https://grc.iit.edu/research/projects/iowarp/>; CLIO Core Jarvis deployment pipelines for Aurora, Delta, and other systems <https://github.com/iowarp/clio-core/tree/v2.2.1/jarvis_clio_core/pipelines>; DeltaAI system at NCSA <https://www.ncsa.illinois.edu/resources-and-services/compute-resources/deltaai/>; CLIO Core source repository <https://github.com/iowarp/clio-core>.

### Agents on scientific data

With IOWarp context, an agent completed EarthScope data retrieval and visualization through the National Data Platform, where a comparison agent without that context did not.
Agent-assisted LAMMPS analysis and IOR deployment finished faster than the same tasks done by hand, across several agent and model combinations. The IEEE eScience 2025 poster states the models, prompts, and timings.
Sources: Islam, Cernuda, Muradli, Kougkas, Sun. Towards an AI-driven scientific workflow. IEEE eScience 2025 (poster) <https://doi.org/10.1109/eScience65000.2025.00074>; eScience 2025 poster PDF: EarthScope, LAMMPS, ParaView, and IOR agent workflows <http://cs.iit.edu/~scs/assets/files/islam2025aidriven_poster.pdf>.

### Data movement and GPUs

GPU kernels submit I/O to CLIO without exiting the kernel, and a workflow-aware compression system chooses a codec for the data at hand. Both are in the CLIO Core source builds.
The team also characterized GPUDirect data transfer through NVIDIA NIXL for AI workloads.
Sources: CLIO Core GPU, compression, and cuFile adapter sources <https://github.com/iowarp/clio-core/tree/v2.4.1/context-transfer-engine/adapter>; Muradli, Ye, Logan, Kougkas, Sun. Insights into GPUDirect data transfer through NIXL benchmarking. IEEE eScience 2025 (poster and extended abstract) <https://doi.org/10.1109/eScience65000.2025.00075>.

### Applications and partnerships

The University of Utah team released the InfiniteScienceGym benchmark. wtf-MS and its CLIO Coder port, Materio, carry materials research planning.
For SPOTTER-AI, CLIO Agent added the Spotter approval mode, and a read-only provenance MCP server in the agent marketplace was qualified against Flowcept and CMF. For PORTUS, the IOWarp team works on workflow motifs and performance models.
Sources: wtf-MS materials research planning system <https://github.com/iowarp/wtf-ms>; Bentham and Srikumar. InfiniteScienceGym: An unbounded, procedurally generated benchmark for scientific analysis. COLM 2026 (arXiv:2604.13201) <https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.13201>; CLIO Agent changelog, including the Spotter approval mode <https://github.com/iowarp/clio-agent/blob/v0.9.6.1/CHANGELOG.md>; CLIO Agent design note: unified Spotter provenance MCP server <https://github.com/iowarp/clio-agent/blob/v0.9.6.1/docs/design/unified-spotter-provenance-mcp-2026-08.md>; Dataflow Performance Matcher: I/O cost prediction across storage tiers and node counts <https://gitlab.com/perflab-exact/dpm/dpm>.

## Applications

### Agents in the materials workflow (https://iowarp.ai/applications/materials-science/)

Partners: University of Utah · Illinois Tech · The HDF Group. Standing: Active collaboration.

The University of Utah team is IOWarp’s primary domain science partner. It contributes materials science workflows and AI research, and those workflows show what the stack has to carry, from a designed part to a defensible account of how it fails.

Question: Can an AI agent carry a materials study from design to simulation to characterization without losing track of the part, the process, and the data?

Where context breaks: A tomography volume is only useful next to the build parameters and the simulation that predicted where the part would crack, yet those live in different places and often only in people’s notebooks. When the Utah team gave an agent domain skills for Abaqus, it could read the models and reason about them, but it could not yet submit, monitor, and retrieve jobs on a remote HPC system. Closing that gap, and keeping one record of each part across every stage, is the stack’s job.

Record:

Next: Integrate wtf-MS so CLIO Agent can use it directly. Run the reference workflow end to end on IOWarp and test it for repeatability against the original, manual study. Extend agent support from topology optimization to tomography characterization and materials data management. Bring InfiniteScienceGym into IOWarp so users can benchmark scientific agents on their own questions.

### Agents on the National Data Platform (https://iowarp.ai/applications/national-data-platform/)

Partners: National Data Platform · University of Utah · Illinois Tech. Standing: Demonstrated on EarthScope data.

The National Data Platform federates scientific data catalogs so researchers can find and use data across institutions. IOWarp builds agent tools on top of it.

Question: Can an agent go from a plain-language request to a staged, analyzed, and plotted dataset from a federated catalog without a human wiring every step?

Where context breaks: The failure mode is missing context: which catalog, which resource, what the columns mean, where the data was staged. CLIO Kit turns each of those into a tool with a defined contract.

Record:
- With IOWarp context, an agent completed EarthScope data retrieval and visualization through NDP; the comparison agent without that context did not complete the workflow. Conditions: Agent runs on Chameleon Cloud, reported in an IEEE eScience 2025 poster that states the models and timings. Sources: Islam, Cernuda, Muradli, Kougkas, Sun. Towards an AI-driven scientific workflow. IEEE eScience 2025 (poster) <https://doi.org/10.1109/eScience65000.2025.00074>.

Next: Publish a repeatable NDP workflow with a pinned catalog snapshot, since live catalogs change between runs. Record the 2026 EarthScope demonstration on current releases. Extend beyond EarthScope to other NDP-federated domains.

### Provenance and integrity for AI-driven science (https://iowarp.ai/applications/genesis-spotter/)

Partners: Argonne National Laboratory · Oak Ridge National Laboratory · Illinois Tech · Hewlett Packard Enterprise. Standing: Project began August 2026.

SPOTTER-AI is a DOE Genesis Mission project. Argonne National Laboratory leads it, with Oak Ridge National Laboratory, Illinois Tech, and Hewlett Packard Enterprise as partners. It addresses cybersecurity for AI-driven science through data provenance and integrity verification. The project began in August 2026. The IOWarp team builds the agents that investigate what the provenance shows.

Question: When a scientific AI workflow produces a wrong answer, can we tell whether it was tampered with, and trace the cause to its source?

Where context breaks: Provenance helps only if someone can question it. The records span workflow events, artifact lineage, and signals from inside the model, across systems never designed to be read together. An investigating agent needs bounded, read-only access to all of it, and its own actions must meet the same standard of evidence.

Record:

Next: Connect the investigation layer to the project’s scientific testbed workflows. Instruction-tune a foundation model for provenance analysis. Record a demonstration of CLIO Agent working with SPOTTER-AI.

### Agentic workflows across HPC and cloud (https://iowarp.ai/applications/genesis-portus/)

Partners: Pacific Northwest National Laboratory · Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory · Iowa State University · University of Delaware · Illinois Tech · collaborating with Oak Ridge National Laboratory and HPE. Standing: Project began August 2026.

PORTUS is a DOE Genesis Mission project at Pacific Northwest National Laboratory. It asks how agentic scientific workflows on the Genesis Mission Platform can be predicted, planned, and adapted while they run across HPC and cloud resources. The project began in August 2026. The IOWarp team works on workflow motifs and performance models.

Question: When an agent rewrites a scientific workflow as it runs, can it know what the new version will cost, and choose a better one, before it runs?

Where context breaks: A coding agent that generates a new workflow fragment needs to know what the fragment will cost on the resources available now: how much data moves between stages, where it waits, and which realization would run better. Surrogate performance models, grounded in memory- and data-centric performance foundations and refined by active learning on live telemetry, give the agent that context. With it the agent can reason about bottlenecks, rank alternatives, and retarget the fragment to the machine, and a domain scientist can describe a workflow in natural language and get a port that performs.

Record:

Next: Build compositional, graph-based surrogate models for recurring workflow motifs. Generate and rank alternative realizations of a workflow: task fusion or decomposition, data staging, synchronous or asynchronous execution, and resource mappings. Close the adaptation loop with active learning on live telemetry. Let a domain scientist describe a workflow in natural language and receive a performant port, with CLIO Coder fleets carrying the work. Record a demonstration of CLIO Coder working with PORTUS.

### CLIO on national research systems (https://iowarp.ai/applications/national-infrastructure/)

Partners: Argonne Leadership Computing Facility · NCSA · The HDF Group · Illinois Tech. Standing: Built and run on national systems.

A context runtime has to work where large-scale science happens. This story records where CLIO Core has been built and run, and how NeuroH5 uses it through its HDF5 connector.

Question: Does the same context runtime build, deploy, and scale across the national machines scientists actually use?

Where context breaks: Deployment itself is context: the scheduler, module stack, network fabric, and storage tiers of each machine. CLIO Core ships Jarvis pipelines that record those choices per system, so a run can be repeated and inspected.

Record:

Next: Publish Aurora scaling data with node configuration and workload stated. Publish DeltaAI transfer-engine measurements with GPU configuration, file system, and workload stated. Record the 2026 demonstration of one Jarvis pipeline deploying CLIO on DeltaAI and Aurora.

### GPU direct I/O and compression (https://iowarp.ai/applications/gpu-data-movement/)

Partners: Illinois Tech Gnosis Research Center · Argonne co-authors on KV-cache research. Standing: Research thread across the stack.

Accelerators changed where scientific data has to be. CLIO Core now reaches into the GPU: kernels submit I/O to IOWarp without leaving the device, GPU-resident data spills to host memory and NVMe, and data can be compressed on the GPU before it moves. The research builds on NVIDIA technologies such as CUDA, cuFile, NIXL, and nvCOMP.

Question: Can scientific data move to and from GPU memory as a first-class tier, without a detour through the CPU?

Where context breaks: The question is the one IOWarp asks at every tier: which data must be next to compute now, and which can wait somewhere cheaper. On a GPU, answering it takes I/O primitives that run inside the kernel and placement that treats GPU memory as the top of the hierarchy.

Record:
- NIXL benchmarking, published at IEEE eScience 2025, characterizes GPUDirect data transfer for AI workloads. Sources: Muradli, Ye, Logan, Kougkas, Sun. Insights into GPUDirect data transfer through NIXL benchmarking. IEEE eScience 2025 (poster and extended abstract) <https://doi.org/10.1109/eScience65000.2025.00075>.

Next: Publish GPU offload measurements with GPU model, interconnect, storage, and workload stated. Bring GPU tests into continuous integration on GPU runners. Record the 2026 demonstration of GPU payload offload with CLIO Core CUDA kernels.

## Research directions

- The GPU as a storage tier (https://iowarp.ai/research/directions/#gpu-tier): Can data reach GPU memory without a detour through the CPU? GPU kernels that issue their own I/O, payloads that spill to host memory and NVMe, compression on the device, and prototypes that give GPUs direct NVMe queues. The question is how far the storage hierarchy can extend into the accelerator. Worked on in: CLIO Core GPU runtime and direct GPU I/O research.
- Context with a lifecycle (https://iowarp.ai/research/directions/#context-lifecycle): What should survive a turn, a handoff, or a project? Working context, handoffs, and durable memory have different lifetimes. Agents need explicit staleness and promotion rules so old notes are never mistaken for current authority. Worked on in: CLIO Coder context continuity.
- Memory as a storage hierarchy (https://iowarp.ai/research/directions/#memory-hierarchy): Which facts belong hot, durable, or replayable? What an agent remembers has different access patterns and lifetimes. The question is how to place, retrieve, and retire it across scientific systems, including the model’s own KV cache. Worked on in: CLIO Agent ARC memory and KV-cache research.
- Staging data while agents think (https://iowarp.ai/research/directions/#staging): Can reasoning time hide I/O time? An agent spends time planning before it reads data. That window can be used to move the data it is likely to request into a faster tier. Worked on in: AgentStage, IEEE eScience 2026.
- Authority that travels with work (https://iowarp.ai/research/directions/#authority): What can a delegated agent actually do? Distributed agents need typed assignments, bounded read and write scopes, and checks that can be inspected after execution. More workers without those controls is not a systems result. Worked on in: CLIO Coder fleet dispatch, with the PORTUS integration in progress.
- Provenance an agent can question (https://iowarp.ai/research/directions/#provenance): When a result is wrong, can we find out why? Provenance spans workflow events, artifact lineage, and signals from inside the model. Investigating agents need read-only access to all of it, and their own actions must be held to the same standard. Worked on in: CLIO Agent provenance investigation, qualified against Flowcept and CMF for SPOTTER-AI.
- Evidence for agentic science (https://iowarp.ai/research/directions/#evidence): What would prove an agent made progress? Scientific workflows need baselines, holdouts, provenance, and run records. A persuasive narrative cannot substitute for measurements tied to their producer and conditions. Worked on in: CLIO Coder research and arena.

## Topics

### Context management for AI agents (https://iowarp.ai/topics/context-management/)

Context management is the work of deciding what an AI agent sees, when, and with what authority: which data, which tool results, which prior decisions, and which limits. For scientific agents it is a systems problem, because the relevant context lives in files, catalogs, schedulers, and instruments.

Why a larger context window is not enough
A model can only reason over what it is given. Handing it everything is slow, expensive, and hides the evidence that matters. Handing it too little makes it improvise. The useful unit is the smallest trustworthy slice of the scientific world needed for the next step.
That slice has several parts with different lifetimes: working context for the current turn, handoffs between agents or sessions, durable project memory, and provenance that must outlive all of them.

Context as a storage hierarchy
Storage systems already solve a similar problem: keep hot data close to compute, move cold data to cheaper tiers, and record where everything is. IOWarp applies the same discipline to agent context. Placement, eviction, and prefetching are as relevant to an agent’s memory as they are to a simulation’s checkpoint files.
The same idea reaches into the model. KV-cache research in the project places and evicts the inference cache like any other tier.

Bounded and inspectable
In science, a result has to be checkable. Context management therefore includes recording what an agent was given and what it was allowed to do, so a reviewer can reconstruct the path from data to claim.

- CLIO Core Python API: Bundle, query, and retrieve context, or work directly with tags, blobs, and search. https://core.iowarp.ai/docs/python-api.html
- CLIO Agent: ARC memory, stored in CLIO Core, carries context across sessions. Each agent loads only the plugins its work needs. https://iowarp.ai/platform/#agent
- CLIO Coder: Guidance for repository context, session handoffs, durable memory, and reviewable run receipts. https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/context-continuity.html
- Anthropic on effective context engineering: Further reading: Curating finite context, retrieving information when needed, and keeping useful state across long tasks. https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents
- OpenAI on managing session context: Further reading: Trimming and summarizing session history, with the tradeoffs in fidelity, latency, and observability. https://developers.openai.com/cookbook/examples/agents_sdk/session_memory
- OpenAI on durable memory and state: Further reading: Capturing durable notes, consolidating them, and resolving precedence between memory and current intent. https://developers.openai.com/cookbook/examples/agents_sdk/context_personalization
- Google DeepMind’s retrieval-augmented language-model research: Further reading: A research example of language models retrieving external text. Retrieval is one part of context management. https://deepmind.google/blog/improving-language-models-by-retrieving-from-trillions-of-tokens/
- Google DeepMind’s GopherCite research: Further reading: Supporting answers with retrieved quotations and abstaining when evidence is insufficient. A citation still needs checking. https://deepmind.google/blog/gophercite-teaching-language-models-to-support-answers-with-verified-quotes/

Q: Is context management the same as retrieval-augmented generation?
A: Retrieval is one mechanism. Context management also covers placement across tiers, lifetimes, authority, and provenance, so the agent’s inputs can be bounded and audited.
Q: Where does IOWarp implement it?
A: CLIO Core provides the runtime and engines; CLIO Agent and CLIO Coder apply it to agent memory and engineering work.
References: Islam, Cernuda, Muradli, Kougkas, Sun. Towards an AI-driven scientific workflow. IEEE eScience 2025 (poster) <https://doi.org/10.1109/eScience65000.2025.00074>; Chitty-Venkata, Ye, Raskar, Kougkas, Sun, Emani, Vishwanath, Nicolae. PagedEviction: Structured block-wise KV cache pruning for efficient LLM inference. Findings of EACL 2026 <https://doi.org/10.18653/v1/2026.findings-eacl.168>; Ye, Maurya, Chitty-Venkata, Nicolae, Kougkas, Sun. PKAS: Predictive KVCache-aware scheduling for faster LLM and transformer inferences. HPDC 2026 <https://doi.org/10.1145/3806645.3807819>; Logan et al., MegaMmap: Blurring the boundary between memory and storage for data-intensive workloads, SC 2024 <https://doi.org/10.1109/SC41406.2024.00114>; Anthropic on effective context engineering <https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents>; OpenAI on managing session context <https://developers.openai.com/cookbook/examples/agents_sdk/session_memory>; OpenAI on durable memory and state <https://developers.openai.com/cookbook/examples/agents_sdk/context_personalization>; Google DeepMind’s retrieval-augmented language-model research <https://deepmind.google/blog/improving-language-models-by-retrieving-from-trillions-of-tokens/>; Google DeepMind’s GopherCite research <https://deepmind.google/blog/gophercite-teaching-language-models-to-support-answers-with-verified-quotes/>.

### Scientific AI agents (https://iowarp.ai/topics/scientific-agents/)

A scientific agent is a language-model-driven program that carries out steps of a research workflow by calling tools: reading datasets, submitting jobs, running analyses, and producing figures. Its value depends less on the model than on the tools it can operate and the context it is given.

What agents are good for today
Agents are effective at the connective work between scientific tools: finding a dataset, checking its structure, configuring a job, turning output into a plot. Demonstrations in the project cover EarthScope data through the National Data Platform, LAMMPS trajectory analysis, ParaView visualization, and IOR deployment.
In the eScience 2025 evaluation, an agent with IOWarp context completed EarthScope retrieval and visualization, while the comparison agent without that context did not complete the workflow.

What stays with scientists
Choosing the question, judging whether a result means anything, and deciding what to publish stay with people. IOWarp agents stage work for review and leave the conclusions to scientists.

Architecture matters
A single agent with every tool attached becomes slow and error-prone. CLIO Agent builds each agent from the marketplace plugins its work needs and delegates sub-tasks to subagents, each with a narrower tool set and context.

- CLIO Agent: Install the scientific data agent, connect a model, and add agents from the marketplace. https://clio.iowarp.ai/docs/install/
- CLIO Kit: The scientific tools agents operate, exposed through the Model Context Protocol. https://iowarp.ai/clio-kit/
- Demonstrations: Public recordings of agent workflows on scientific data and HPC tools. https://iowarp.ai/research/demos/
- Anthropic on building effective agents: Further reading: Distinguishing workflows from autonomous agents, and choosing simple, composable patterns. https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents
- Anthropic’s multi-agent research architecture: Further reading: An orchestrator and specialized research workers, with lessons about coordination, evaluation, and reliability. https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system

Q: Which models does IOWarp require?
A: None in particular. The software is designed to work with institutional, local, and commercial models; demonstrations have used several agent and model combinations.
Q: Are the agents autonomous?
A: Operators set how much runs without approval through approval modes and permission gates. A CLIO Coder research campaign keeps each accepted change on its own branch, and a person reviews and merges it.
References: Islam, Cernuda, Muradli, Kougkas, Sun. Towards an AI-driven scientific workflow. IEEE eScience 2025 (poster) <https://doi.org/10.1109/eScience65000.2025.00074>; eScience 2025 poster PDF: EarthScope, LAMMPS, ParaView, and IOR agent workflows <http://cs.iit.edu/~scs/assets/files/islam2025aidriven_poster.pdf>; Agent examining EarthScope data through the National Data Platform (video, October 2025) <https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9NUf76wnHhA>; Anthropic on building effective agents <https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents>; Anthropic’s multi-agent research architecture <https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system>.

### MCP servers for scientific computing (https://iowarp.ai/topics/mcp-for-science/)

The Model Context Protocol is an open standard through which AI applications call external tools and read external resources. An MCP server wraps a capability, such as reading an HDF5 dataset or submitting a Slurm job, behind a described interface any compatible client can use.

Why science needs its own servers
General-purpose tools do not understand hierarchical scientific formats, job schedulers, I/O traces, or domain catalogs. A server that knows how to list HDF5 groups or parse a Darshan log gives an agent precise operations instead of guesswork over raw bytes.

HDF5 with agents
HDF5 is a standard format for simulation and experimental data across the sciences. CLIO Kit’s HDF5 server lets an agent list groups, inspect datasets and attributes, and read slices without pulling whole files, and CLIO Core’s HDF5 VOL connector lets existing HDF5 applications place data through the runtime without code changes.
The HDF Group works on agentic HDF5 and agent skills with the IOWarp team, and a birds-of-a-feather session at SC26 will cover HDF5 in AI-driven science.

What CLIO Kit provides
CLIO Kit is an open-source meta-marketplace of scientific MCP servers, skills, agents, hooks, and workflow plugins. Its servers cover data formats (HDF5, Parquet, ADIOS, Pandas), HPC operations (Slurm, Spack, Lmod, Jarvis, Darshan, node hardware), visualization (ParaView, Plot), geospatial and seismic data, and discovery (ArXiv, NDP, scientific catalogs, web search).
The launcher installs from PyPI as clio-kit and downloads selected components on demand. Project installers support Codex, Claude Code, OpenCode, Cursor, Antigravity, and VS Code; agents and hooks have client-specific adapters and limits.

Design choices
Each server is separately versioned and testable, so a facility can adopt only the servers it trusts. Component downloads are verified, and server dependencies stay isolated and locked. Tools return structured results, which makes an agent’s steps easier to check afterward. The HDF5, ADIOS, Pandas, Parquet, and Slurm servers gained tool behavior found by running them through CLIO Coder on planted scientific datasets.

- CLIO Kit catalog: Every server, grouped by capability, with install commands. https://iowarp.ai/clio-kit/
- Connect an MCP client: Register CLIO Kit servers in Claude Code, Cursor, VS Code, and other clients. https://iowarp.ai/clio-kit/#connect
- CLIO Kit guides: Component setup, workflow plugins, and client guides. https://toolkit.iowarp.ai/docs/intro
- Kit client support: Choose skills, MCP configuration, agents, and hooks that your client supports. https://toolkit.iowarp.ai/docs/clients#component-support
- Anthropic’s introduction to MCP: Further reading: Why an open protocol connects AI applications to external data and capabilities. https://www.anthropic.com/news/model-context-protocol
- Anthropic on designing effective tools: Further reading: Designing precise tool interfaces and useful results, then evaluating whether agents can operate them. https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/writing-tools-for-agents

Q: How do I install a CLIO Kit server?
A: Install the launcher with uv tool install clio-kit, then run clio-kit mcp-server followed by the server name. It downloads that component and prepares its isolated runtime. Register the command in your MCP client, or use a workflow plugin to install its MCP configuration and skills together.
Q: Is CLIO Kit tied to one AI vendor?
A: No. It implements the open MCP standard and is documented for several clients.
References: CLIO Kit source repository <https://github.com/iowarp/clio-kit>; CLIO Kit NDP MCP server documentation <https://toolkit.iowarp.ai/docs/mcps/ndp>; ParaView MCP server in CLIO Kit, derived from LLNL paraview_mcp <https://github.com/iowarp/clio-kit/tree/v2.12.3/mcp-servers/paraview>; Islam, Cernuda, Muradli, Kougkas, Sun. Towards an AI-driven scientific workflow. IEEE eScience 2025 (poster) <https://doi.org/10.1109/eScience65000.2025.00074>; Model Context Protocol specification and documentation <https://modelcontextprotocol.io/>; HDF5, The HDF Group <https://www.hdfgroup.org/solutions/hdf5/>; Anthropic’s introduction to MCP <https://www.anthropic.com/news/model-context-protocol>; Anthropic on designing effective tools <https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/writing-tools-for-agents>.

### HPC I/O and storage hierarchies (https://iowarp.ai/topics/hpc-io/)

HPC I/O research studies how applications read and write data on supercomputers: through memory, burst buffers, node-local flash, parallel file systems, and archives. The deep memory and storage hierarchy is fast only if data is in the right tier at the right time.

Where IOWarp comes from
IOWarp builds on Hermes, an earlier system for multi-tiered distributed I/O buffering, and on a line of Gnosis Research Center systems for labeled I/O, time-ordered logging, and data-task scheduling. The founding aim: bending the I/O fabric for AI-infused scientific workflows.

Measured results in the line of work
MegaMmap (SC 2024) manages DRAM and storage as tiered distributed shared memory and lowered peak DRAM use while keeping performance competitive. WisIO (ICS 2025) automates I/O bottleneck detection in HPC workflows. The papers state the workloads and figures.

Why it matters for agents
Agents add a new kind of client to the storage stack: many small, latency-sensitive reads guided by reasoning. The CLIO transfer engine carries the tiering ideas into that setting.

- Storage and context: How CLIO Core’s transfer engine places data across tiers. https://iowarp.ai/platform/#layer-storage
- Where results live: Papers, release notes, and project sites that carry the measurements with their conditions. https://iowarp.ai/progress/#where-results-live
- Research archive: Publications behind the systems lineage. https://iowarp.ai/research/
- Compose storage tiers: Configure local tiers and inspect how the Core filesystem uses its storage chain. https://core.iowarp.ai/tutorials/compose.html

Q: Does IOWarp replace the parallel file system?
A: No. It sits alongside existing storage and manages data flow across tiers during a workflow.
Q: Which I/O interfaces does CLIO Core intercept?
A: In source builds, the transfer engine has adapters for POSIX, STDIO, HDF5 (VOL and VFD), and FUSE, an optional MPI-IO adapter, and GPU paths.
References: Logan et al., MegaMmap: Blurring the boundary between memory and storage for data-intensive workloads, SC 2024 <https://doi.org/10.1109/SC41406.2024.00114>; Yildirim et al., WisIO: Automated I/O bottleneck detection with multi-perspective views for HPC workflows, ICS 2025 <https://doi.org/10.1145/3721145.3725742>; Tang, Guo, Kougkas, Sun, Tallent. Characterizing dataflow for I/O-aware scheduling in HPC workflows. IPDPS 2026 <https://doi.org/10.1109/IPDPS65963.2026.00076>.

### Data movement for AI-infused workflows (https://iowarp.ai/topics/data-movement/)

Scientific data rarely starts where it will be used. It moves from instruments and repositories to HPC storage, between memory and storage tiers, and into GPU memory for AI workloads. Each move costs time and loses context unless it is managed.

Ingestion with meaning attached
The CLIO assimilation engine brings data in from local and parallel file systems and from Globus endpoints, described by OMNI files that record what the data is and how to read it.

Placement and staging
The transfer engine places data across tiers using selectable placement policies. Research in the project goes further: AgentStage at eScience 2026 uses an agent’s own reasoning time as a window to move requested data into place.

Into the GPU
Student work characterizes GPU-direct transfer through NVIDIA NIXL, and the transfer engine includes GPU-aware paths for accelerated workloads.

- CLIO Core: Assimilation, transfer, and exploration engines. https://iowarp.ai/platform/#core
- GPU data movement: NIXL, CUDA integration, and KV-cache research. https://iowarp.ai/applications/gpu-data-movement/
- Install and configure CLIO Core: Published wheels, the conda channel, source builds, and system prerequisites. https://core.iowarp.ai/docs/installation.html

Q: Can CLIO pull data from Globus?
A: Yes, through the assimilation engine’s Globus support in source builds. An end-to-end integration test passes on a public Globus collection.
References: Muradli, Ye, Logan, Kougkas, Sun. Insights into GPUDirect data transfer through NIXL benchmarking. IEEE eScience 2025 (poster and extended abstract) <https://doi.org/10.1109/eScience65000.2025.00075>; IEEE eScience 2026 accepted papers, including Acropolis and AgentStage <https://www.escience-conference.org/2026/papers>; CLIO Core Globus materials-science assimilation test <https://github.com/iowarp/clio-core/tree/v2.4.1/context-assimilation-engine/test/integration/globus_matsci>.

### Scientific workflows and reproducible deployment (https://iowarp.ai/topics/scientific-workflows/)

A scientific workflow chains simulation, analysis, AI, and visualization steps across machines. It is only useful as evidence if another person can run it again and get an explainable result.

Deployment as a record
Jarvis describes a software stack and its resources as a pipeline that can be deployed, monitored, and torn down. CLIO Core ships pipelines for Aurora, Delta, local machines, and other targets, so a run records its own configuration.

Integrations
The workflow integration catalog covers simulations such as LAMMPS and Gray-Scott, storage services, and I/O benchmarks such as IOR and FIO.

Agent-operated steps
When an agent performs a step, the tool calls and their results become part of the workflow record. The IOR deployment evaluation in the eScience 2025 poster measured agents configuring the benchmark across several agent and model combinations and prompt variations.

- Jarvis: Deployment pipelines and packages for simulations, services, and benchmarks. https://iowarp.ai/platform/#jarvis
- Application stories: Materials science, the National Data Platform, DOE Genesis Mission projects, and national systems. https://iowarp.ai/applications/
- CLIO Kit: Slurm, Spack, and Jarvis servers that let an agent operate the workflow’s schedulers and deployments. https://iowarp.ai/clio-kit/

Q: What is Jarvis?
A: A deployment framework from the Gnosis Research Center that describes software stacks as pipelines over a resource graph. CLIO Core uses it for per-machine deployment.
References: Cernuda et al., Jarvis: Towards a shared, user-friendly, and reproducible I/O infrastructure, PDSW 2024 work-in-progress session (Work-in-progress presentation); CLIO Core Jarvis deployment pipelines for Aurora, Delta, and other systems <https://github.com/iowarp/clio-core/tree/v2.2.1/jarvis_clio_core/pipelines>; eScience 2025 poster PDF: EarthScope, LAMMPS, ParaView, and IOR agent workflows <http://cs.iit.edu/~scs/assets/files/islam2025aidriven_poster.pdf>; Tang, Guo, Kougkas, Sun, Tallent. Characterizing dataflow for I/O-aware scheduling in HPC workflows. IPDPS 2026 <https://doi.org/10.1109/IPDPS65963.2026.00076>; WfCommons: open workflow instances and tools <https://wfcommons.org/>.

### Evidence-based autonomous research (https://iowarp.ai/topics/evidence-based-research/)

Autonomous research systems propose changes and test them. Their output is only as credible as the measurement discipline behind it: a fixed baseline, repeated trials, a holdout the system did not tune against, and a record of every run.

The failure mode
A system that generates both the change and the explanation can produce a persuasive narrative for a result that does not replicate. Evidence has to come from measurements tied to the conditions that produced them.

How IOWarp is approaching it
clio-coder research runs a budgeted hill climb on one measured number in a project. It measures the base against itself to establish the noise, lets the agent propose a change in a fresh worktree, compares candidate and base in interleaved trials, and keeps the change only when a bootstrap interval excludes zero and every correctness gate passes. Kept changes land on a separate branch for a person to review and merge, and research report regrades every verdict from the raw samples. clio-coder arena gives one prompt to several models side by side and hides their identities until you vote. Neither command asks a model to judge quality.

- CLIO Coder research and arena: Declare an objective and its gates, run a campaign, and compare models blind. https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/research-and-arena.html
- Results and milestones: What the project has built, run, measured, and published. https://iowarp.ai/progress/
- Anthropic on evaluating agents: Further reading: Evaluating agent outcomes, tool calls, and traces with deterministic, model-based, and human graders. https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents
- OpenAI’s evaluation flywheel: Further reading: Diagnosing failure cases, establishing a baseline, and measuring targeted improvements. https://github.com/openai/openai-cookbook/blob/main/examples/evaluation/Building_resilient_prompts_using_an_evaluation_flywheel.md
- Google DeepMind’s AlphaEvolve research: Further reading: A coding-agent research system that proposes executable candidates and scores them with automated evaluators. https://deepmind.google/blog/alphaevolve-a-gemini-powered-coding-agent-for-designing-advanced-algorithms/

Q: Can I run a research campaign now?
A: Yes. Install CLIO Coder, declare a metric and its correctness checks in the project’s verifier catalog, and run clio-coder research start with an iteration limit.
References: IEEE eScience 2026 accepted papers, including Acropolis and AgentStage <https://www.escience-conference.org/2026/papers>; Yildirim et al., WisIO: Automated I/O bottleneck detection with multi-perspective views for HPC workflows, ICS 2025 <https://doi.org/10.1145/3721145.3725742>; Anthropic on evaluating agents <https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents>; OpenAI’s evaluation flywheel <https://github.com/openai/openai-cookbook/blob/main/examples/evaluation/Building_resilient_prompts_using_an_evaluation_flywheel.md>; Google DeepMind’s AlphaEvolve research <https://deepmind.google/blog/alphaevolve-a-gemini-powered-coding-agent-for-designing-advanced-algorithms/>.
